330.title: The ranges ahead
330.hook: four more years: the Stoics in full, the great questions, the thinkers and the practices, and your own way
330.howItsDone: People on a long path of study often pause at the end of a year to look ahead at what comes next, without committing to all of it at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you still don't know. Your line was still asking. Did you say I don't know out loud, once, when it was true? Keep those three questions. Day three hundred thirty.

When you finally reach the top of a hill, there's a moment everyone who hikes knows. You catch your breath, you look out, and you see that this wasn't the top of anything. Behind it, there's another ridge. Behind that, a range. Blue, then paler blue, all the way to the edge of the sky. For some people that moment is deflating. More climbing? For others it's the best part of the whole walk. The world is bigger than the hill. Tomorrow, year one ends. Today, before we look back down one last time, we look out. Today: the ranges ahead.
screen: `THE TOP OF THE HILL.` → `ANOTHER RIDGE, THEN A RANGE.` → `BIGGER THAN THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Here's what the next four years look like, ridge by ridge. First, year two: the porch. The Stoics in full. We met them in stories and practices; next year we read them properly, starting with Epictetus's handbook, in order, a line at a time. The school took its name from the stoa, the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught, so year two is named for it. Second, year three: the great questions. Wisdom from every tradition, gathered by theme. What is a good life? How do we face death? What do we owe each other? Each tradition answers in its own words, and we'll listen to each without ranking them, the way we did this year as guests. Third, year four: the thinkers and the schools. It opens with the Tao Te Ching, chapter by chapter, the old master's short, strange book, and goes on to the philosophers and the practices that grew around them. Fourth, year five: the summit. Reading the sources yourself, walking with the poets, and finally, living your own way. By then, the path hands you less and asks more. The questions you wrote yesterday will still be there. A few may have softened. Here's the honest part. Nobody knows how far you'll go. Some people walk the whole range. Some walk a year, and carry two practices for the rest of their lives, and that is a whole life's worth. The ranges aren't a to-do list. They're there, the way mountains are there: to look at, to wonder at, and to walk when you're ready. One day at a time, like this one.
screen: `YEAR TWO: THE PORCH.` · `YEAR THREE: THE GREAT QUESTIONS.` · `YEAR FOUR: THE THINKERS AND THE SCHOOLS.` · `YEAR FIVE: THE SUMMIT.` · then, large: `THE RANGES.`

segments.voice: Look at the horizon. Go to a window, or outside, and find the farthest thing you can see: a line of roofs, trees, hills, the sky's edge. Let your eyes rest there, soft and wide. Notice how far away it is. Then notice your breath, right here. The far thing and the near breath, both at once. Don't plan anything. Just look out. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. Four more years: the porch, the great questions, the thinkers and the schools, and the summit. Today's word.
Your line: the ranges. Once today, look at the farthest thing you can see, and let it be far. No need to reach it today. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: year one ends: look back down the hill, then up
331.howItsDone: Many people mark the end of a long stretch of practice by going somewhere high or open, looking back over what they did, and naming what comes next.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ranges ahead. Your line was the ranges. Did you find the farthest thing you could see, and let it be far? Day three hundred thirty-one. The last day of year one.

Picture the lookout at the top of the hill. A flat rock, a rail, maybe a bench someone carved their initials into. You've been climbing for three hundred thirty-one days. Some of them you ran. Some of them you crawled. A few you sat down on the path and didn't move, and that counted too. Now you're here. Below you, the whole trail, switchbacks and all, back down to the spot where you took one breath with a bell. Above and beyond, the ranges. You get to stand in the middle, for one day, and see both. Today: the big lookout.
screen: `A FLAT ROCK, A RAIL, A BENCH.` → `331 DAYS OF CLIMBING.` → `THE TRAIL BELOW, THE RANGES BEYOND.`

segments.voice: First, look down at the camps. The first words, starting with breathe. The stories: a shipwreck, a butterfly, a carob tree. The practices: the breath, the evening review, the sunset. The text: Rumi's reed, with Marcus beside him. Second, look down at this last camp, the depths, the longest of all. We went as guests into seven homes. Hinduism: dharma, and you are that. Buddhism: wake up, and may all beings be well. Judaism: hear, and repair. Christianity: love your neighbor, and grace. The Catholic tradition: the rosary and the works of mercy. Islam: one God, and hearts that find rest in remembrance. Sikhism: the name, honest work, and the free kitchen. Then home to the Stoic porch: character, the four virtues, the citadel. Then the lab: six breaths a minute, sixty-six days, green helps, sleep first, and what science can't say. Third, a line from a tradition that loved hills. A psalm, in the King James words: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." For the psalmist, the help comes from God, the maker of heaven and earth. Hills are where people have always gone to look up. Fourth, a line from the Tao Te Ching, in James Legge's translation: "The journey of a thousand li commences with a single step." You took that step on day one. Every step since was also a single step. That's all a year is. Look how far. Tomorrow, the porch: year two opens with a little handbook meant to be kept at hand.
screen: `WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, THE TEXT.` · `SEVEN HOMES, THE PORCH, THE LAB.` · `I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.` · `A THOUSAND LI, A SINGLE STEP.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Stand somewhere high, if you can: a hill, a balcony, the top of the stairs. Or go to a window. First, look down. Let the year pass below you: a face, a story, a hard week, a good one. Then take one breath, the same breath as day one. Now look up and out, as far as you can see. Stay there, between the two. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The top of year one: look back down the whole trail, then up at the ranges. Today's word, and the last of the year.
Your line: look how far. Tell one person tonight that you finished a year of this. Then rest. Tomorrow, the porch. Day three hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HANDBOOK FOR THE ROAD.`
